items.title: The earliest Christians thought Jesus would return within their lifetime
items.claim: Paul's letters (50s CE) are the oldest Christian texts. What does he tell his churches about the timing of Christ's return?

options.text: He explicitly warns that it will be many centuries away
He tells believers — in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 — that 'we who are alive, who are left' will be caught up to meet the Lord
He refuses to discuss the timing at all
He places the return precisely at AD 70, the destruction of the Temple

items.reveal:
1 Thessalonians 4:15-17, written around 50-51 CE, includes Paul among those still alive at the Parousia. 1 Corinthians 7:29 says 'the appointed time has grown short.' Mark 9:1 has Jesus saying 'some standing here will not taste death' before seeing the Kingdom.

When Christ did not return, later texts (e.g. 2 Peter 3:8 — 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years') reinterpret the delay. This shift is one of the central transformations of early Christian theology.
items.why: Treating the New Testament as a unified, settled doctrine misses that it documents a community reinterpreting itself in real time. The 'delay of the Parousia' is one of the formative pressures on Christian thought.

items.title: Buddhism teaches anatta — no permanent self
items.claim: What is the doctrine of anatta?

options.text: The soul is eternal and unchanging
There is no permanent, unchanging self (atman); what we call 'self' is a constantly changing aggregation of five skandhas (form, feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness)
Only the body is real; the soul is illusion

items.reveal:
Anatta (no-self) is one of the three marks of existence in Buddhism, alongside anicca (impermanence) and dukkha (unsatisfactoriness). The doctrine sharply distinguishes Buddhism from Hinduism's atman/Brahman teaching.

The Anattalakkhana Sutta — the Buddha's second sermon — argues each of the five skandhas is impermanent and not under our control, so cannot be 'self'.

Later Mahayana schools developed the concept further. Yogacara introduced 'alaya-vijnana' (storehouse consciousness); some Pure Land traditions speak of 'Buddha-nature' that complicates the picture without abandoning anatta.
items.why: Anatta is one of the most counter-intuitive religious doctrines. It contradicts both Western theological assumptions about the soul and lived experience of continuity — and is the central philosophical claim of Buddhism.

items.title: Paley's watchmaker argument was published in 1802

options.text: If we found a stone on a heath, we would infer no designer
If we found a watch on a heath, the complexity and purposive arrangement of its parts would compel us to infer a watchmaker — and similar reasoning applied to nature implies a divine designer
Nature is too random to need a designer
The argument compares the universe to a clockwork mechanism explicitly

items.reveal:
William Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) opens with the watch-on-the-heath analogy. He uses the human eye as his prime biological example.

Hume's 'Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion' (1779, published posthumously) anticipated and refuted versions of the design argument decades earlier — the analogy is weak (the universe is not like a watch), there are flaws (suggesting an apprentice designer or a committee), and the argument cannot reach a single benevolent God.

Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) provided a non-design explanation for biological complexity. Modern Intelligent Design (Behe, Dembski, 1990s onwards) is a controversial attempt to revive the argument scientifically.
items.why: The design argument keeps returning in new forms. Each version has to deal with the next development in science — biological evolution, cosmic fine-tuning, multiverse cosmology — making it a moving target rather than a settled debate.
